subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Pooja. When Bidisha joined our class from Sydney, I thought she was the most unsure person I'd ever met. Everything she said went up at the end. “I live near the temple? My dad's a nurse? I like drawing?” I kept answering, “Yes? Okay?” as if she'd asked me something. Once she said, “The answer is forty-two?” and I told her not to worry, it was probably right. She gave me a funny look. “I know it's right.” Later she explained that where she grew up, lots of people talk like that, even when they're sure. Now I listen to her face, not just the end of her sentences.

qa.q: Where did Bidisha join the class from?
qa.a: Bidisha joined from Sydney.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Pooja said the answer was probably right?
qa.a: Bidisha felt puzzled and perhaps a bit annoyed, since she was sure and the rising tone was just her way of speaking.

qa.q: What does Pooja do now, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Pooja listens to Bidisha's face as well as the tone, since a rising ending can be a habit rather than doubt.

qa.q: What would change if Pooja had never learned about the habit?
qa.a: Pooja might keep treating Bidisha as unsure, which could feel patronising to someone who is actually confident.

grounding: Shows a child reading a rising voice as doubt, and learning it can be a regional speaking habit instead.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: Class note, Thursday. Minakshi, Class 5 science. Ankita answers almost everything with her voice going up at the end: “Chlorophyll? Sunlight?” For weeks I took this as doubt and kept giving her more hints. Today I asked her privately if she was unsure. She looked surprised. “No, Ma'am. At home we're told not to sound too sure in front of elders. It's rude.” That was new to me. Her answers are nearly always right. I explained that in class a falling voice simply says “this is my answer”, and it isn't rude. She tried it: “Chlorophyll.” Down at the end. She smiled. I've stopped giving her hints she doesn't need.

qa.q: What did Ankita's family teach about sounding sure?
qa.a: They taught her not to sound too sure in front of elders, because it's rude.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when Minakshi asked if she was unsure?
qa.a: Ankita felt surprised, since she was confident; the rising tone was politeness, not doubt.

qa.q: What did Minakshi change after the talk?
qa.a: Minakshi explained that a falling tone isn't rude in class and stopped giving Ankita hints she didn't need.

qa.q: How had Minakshi read the rising tone for weeks?
qa.a: Minakshi took it as doubt and kept offering hints, not knowing it was a politeness habit.

grounding: Shows a teacher reading a child's rising tone as doubt when it was politeness taught at home, and context changing the meaning.

subtype: Rising pitch for questions and doubt [Interpreting]
passage: Wednesday. Nazia's diary. Ritu sent a voice note about the science fair: “I'll bring the batteries? And I'll come at eight?” Her voice went up at the end of everything. I didn't know if she was asking me or telling me. Is she even sure she's coming? I nearly asked Aapi to take me instead. Then I just called her. “Ritu, are you coming at eight or not?” She laughed. “Yes, definitely! I always sound like that on voice notes. My mum says I sound like I'm asking permission.” So I stopped worrying. She came at five to eight, with the batteries.

qa.q: What did Ritu say she would bring?
qa.a: Ritu said she would bring the batteries.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling after the voice note?
qa.a: Nazia felt uncertain and a little worried that Ritu might not be sure about coming.

qa.q: Why was calling Ritu a good idea?
qa.a: It checked the meaning directly, showing the rising tone was Ritu's usual habit, not doubt.

qa.q: How does Ritu's mother describe Ritu's voice notes?
qa.a: Ritu's mother says she sounds like she's asking permission, which shows the rising tone is a habit.

grounding: Shows a child reading a friend's rising tone as doubt, and checking to find it was a speaking habit.

passage: Monday. Aditi's diary. My voice is a frog today. I screamed so much at Saturday's kabaddi final that now I can only croak. In class, when Deepika asked to borrow my compass, I said, “Take it,” and it came out rough and low. She pulled her hand back. “Why are you angry with me?” I wasn't! I tried to explain, and it came out even more like a growl, and she looked hurt. So I wrote in my rough book: NOT ANGRY. LOST MY VOICE SHOUTING FOR OUR TEAM. She read it and burst out laughing. Ma'am let me write my answers today. I'm drinking warm water with honey.

qa.q: What made Aditi lose the voice?
qa.a: Aditi screamed a lot at Saturday's kabaddi final.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she pulled her hand back?
qa.a: Deepika felt hurt and worried, reading Aditi's rough, low voice as anger at her.

qa.q: What did Aditi do to fix the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Aditi wrote a clear note explaining the voice was lost from shouting, not anger.

qa.q: What would change if Aditi had just stayed silent?
qa.a: Deepika might have gone on believing Aditi was angry with her, and felt hurt all day.

grounding: Shows a raspy voice from shouting being misread as anger, when voice quality reflects body state first.

passage: Chinmay had a heavy cold, and when Deepika Teacher asked him to read the poem aloud in the village school, it came out thick and nasal: “The bango tree by our dore.” Three boys at the back honked like geese. Chinmay's ears went red, and he stopped. Deepika Teacher put down her chalk. “His nose is blocked. That's all a voice like that means: a cold, not a joke. Mine sounded the same last week.” She poured Chinmay a cup of warm water from her flask. “Read again when you're ready.” He finished the poem. The boys stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Deepika Teacher give Chinmay?
qa.a: She poured him a cup of warm water from her flask.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling when the boys honked?
qa.a: Chinmay felt embarrassed and hurt, his ears going red, so he stopped reading.

qa.q: How did Deepika Teacher handle the mocking?
qa.a: She stopped the lesson, explained that a nasal voice means a cold, shared that hers sounded the same, and let Chinmay continue when ready.

qa.q: How did the boys at the back read Chinmay's voice?
qa.a: They treated the nasal voice as something funny to mock, not realising it simply came from a blocked nose.

grounding: Shows peers mocking a child's nasal voice from a cold, and a teacher explaining that voice quality is body state first.

passage: Every spring in Hanoi, Tuan's voice went scratchy and rough, like sandpaper. Aiko, who had only moved there in January, didn't know that. When she asked if he wanted to be partners for the science poster, he croaked, “Sure, fine,” and coughed. Aiko's face fell. He sounds so grumpy. Maybe he doesn't want to work with me. She almost asked someone else. Then she noticed his red, watery eyes and the tissues piled on his desk. “Are you sick?” “Allergies,” he rasped. “The flowers outside. I'm happy to be partners, I promise. My voice just sounds cross.” Aiko laughed and pushed the window shut.

qa.q: When does Tuan's voice go scratchy?
qa.a: Every spring in Hanoi, Tuan's voice goes scratchy and rough.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when Tuan croaked his answer?
qa.a: Aiko felt disappointed and worried that Tuan didn't want to work with her, reading the rough voice as grumpiness.

qa.q: What clues helped Aiko read the voice correctly?
qa.a: Tuan's red, watery eyes and the pile of tissues showed he was unwell, so she asked instead of assuming.

qa.q: How does Tuan feel about his spring voice?
qa.a: Tuan knows his voice sounds cross during allergy season, which is why he promised Aiko he was happy to be partners.

grounding: Shows a raspy voice from allergies being misread as grumpiness, when it reflects body state, not mood.

passage: Monday: Payal's science model had been crushed on the bus. When Chandrika Ma'am asked where it was, Payal answered in a tight, high voice: “I. Don't. Have it.” “Don't take that tone with me,” Ma'am snapped. Payal's throat locked, and she said nothing more. Wednesday: At the water cooler, Chandrika Ma'am found Payal with her jaw clenched and eyes shining. This time she heard the strain differently. She handed her a cup. “Sip. Breathe out slowly with me.” After three breaths, Payal said in her normal voice, “Someone sat on it on the bus.” Friday: They rebuilt the model together at lunch, and Ma'am apologised for Monday.

qa.q: What happened to Payal's science model?
qa.a: It was crushed on the bus when someone sat on it.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when she spoke in a tight, high voice on Monday?
qa.a: Payal was upset and holding back tears about her crushed model, and the strain was her effort to stay composed.

qa.q: What did Chandrika Ma'am do on Wednesday that helped?
qa.a: She handed Payal water and breathed out slowly with her, which loosened her voice so she could explain.

qa.q: How did Chandrika Ma'am first hear Payal's voice?
qa.a: At first she heard the strained voice as rudeness and snapped, missing that Payal was trying to cope.

grounding: Shows a child's tight, strained voice while holding back tears, and water and slow breathing loosening it once an adult reads it as coping.

passage: Pranav, when you answered me just now in that tight voice, you sounded exactly like your father at ten. Let your Lakshmi Paati tell you. His best friend had moved away to Delhi that morning. When I asked him to set the table, he said, “I. Will. Do it. Later,” every word squeezed. My mother-in-law said, “Such cheek!” But I saw his chin wobbling. I didn't argue. I poured him a glass of water, sat beside him and breathed slowly, loud enough for him to copy. After a few breaths his voice came back, soft and wet: “I miss Ravi.” We sat there a long while. The table got set later.

qa.q: Where had the best friend moved to?
qa.a: His best friend had moved away to Delhi.

qa.q: What was the boy feeling as he squeezed out each word?
qa.a: He was sad and holding back tears about his best friend leaving, and the strain was his effort to cope.

qa.q: What choice did Lakshmi make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She didn't argue but gave him water and breathed slowly beside him, which loosened his voice so he could say he missed Ravi.

qa.q: How did the boy's grandmother read his voice?
qa.a: She heard it as cheek, missing the wobbling chin that showed he was close to tears.

grounding: Shows a child's strained voice while holding back tears being read as cheek, and water and slow breathing helping.

passage: The inter-school quiz was in its final round, with thirty seconds per answer and the whole hall watching. When the other team's captain muttered, “They must have seen the questions,” Lalremsiami's face went hot. Her turn came. “The capital of… of Mongolia is…” Her voice came out tight and thin, as if squeezed through a straw. The quizmaster frowned. Keerthana, her teammate, slid the water bottle across and whispered, “Sip. Breathe out long.” Lalremsiami did, once. “Ulaanbaatar,” she said, steadier. The quizmaster nodded and added gently, “Take your time. That was a hard moment.” Afterwards he spoke to the other captain about the remark.

qa.q: How long did teams have per answer?
qa.a: Teams had thirty seconds per answer.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when her voice came out tight and thin?
qa.a: She was angry and hurt at being accused of cheating and was fighting to hold it in during her turn.

qa.q: How did Keerthana help under the time pressure?
qa.a: Keerthana passed water and whispered to breathe out long, which steadied Lalremsiami's voice enough to answer.

qa.q: How did the quizmaster come to read the strain?
qa.a: After a frown, he saw it as effort to cope with a hard moment, reassured her and later spoke to the other captain.

grounding: Shows a child's voice going tight while holding back anger, and water and slow breathing helping, with an adult reading it as coping.

passage: I'm Manoj, from the flat next door, and I was pumping my cycle tyre on the landing when Hafsa came home from school. Her Ammi opened the door. “How was the test?” “Fine.” “Did you eat your lunch?” “Yes.” “And the bus?” “Okay.” Hafsa walked straight in and dropped her bag. I thought her Ammi would push, like mine does. She didn't. She just said, “There's chai when you want it,” and went back to the kitchen. About half an hour later, through the open window, I heard Hafsa's voice, long and wobbly, telling her Ammi everything about the test. I don't know what happened in it, but she was talking.

qa.q: What was Manoj doing on the landing?
qa.a: Manoj was pumping a cycle tyre.

qa.q: What was Hafsa likely feeling when she gave one-word answers?
qa.a: Hafsa was likely tired or upset after the test and not ready to talk yet.

qa.q: Why did Ammi's response work?
qa.a: She didn't demand details but offered chai and time, so Hafsa could come and talk when ready.

qa.q: How does Manoj compare Hafsa's Ammi with Manoj's own mother?
qa.a: Manoj expected Ammi to push the way Manoj's mother does, and was surprised she gave Hafsa space.

grounding: Shows a child's clipped replies after a hard day, and an adult offering time and a low-pressure moment instead of demanding detail.

passage: Monday: Sonali came in from dance class and answered every question with one word. “Good.” “No.” “Tired.” Rehana Khala kept asking. “What happened? Tell me. Why are you like this?” Sonali shut her bedroom door. Tuesday: Rehana didn't ask anything. After dinner she said, “I'm walking to the shop for milk. Want to come?” They walked in silence past the lit-up shops. Near the paan stall, Sonali said, “They took me out of the front row for the show.” Rehana just listened. Thursday: Sonali practised her steps in the living room and asked Rehana to watch.

qa.q: What did Rehana walk to the shop for?
qa.a: Rehana walked to the shop for milk.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling behind her one-word answers on Monday?
qa.a: She was hurt and disappointed about being taken out of the front row, and not ready to talk.

qa.q: What changed on Tuesday that helped Sonali open up?
qa.a: Rehana stopped questioning and offered a quiet walk, a low-pressure moment when Sonali could talk if she wanted.

qa.q: What would change if Rehana had kept pushing on Tuesday?
qa.a: Sonali might have stayed behind her closed door and never shared the hurt about the dance show.

grounding: Shows an adult learning that a child's clipped replies need time and a low-pressure moment rather than demands for detail.

passage: Vidya, when you say “fine” like that, I hear your mother at eleven. Let your Shankar Thatha tell you. One week she came home and every answer was clipped. “Fine.” “Nothing.” “Don't know.” I kept pushing, and she kept closing like a door. Then your Paati told me, “Stop asking. Just be there.” So one evening I sat on the steps oiling my cycle chain and said nothing. She came and sat, and after a long while she told me some girls had been calling her names because of her glasses. I thanked her for telling me. The same evening I phoned her class teacher, who spoke to those girls the very next morning.

qa.q: What was Thatha oiling on the steps?
qa.a: He was oiling his cycle chain.

qa.q: What was the girl feeling behind her clipped answers?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed by the name-calling about her glasses and not ready to talk.

qa.q: What choice did Thatha make after Paati's advice, and why did it work?
qa.a: He stopped asking and simply sat near her, a low-pressure moment that let her share the problem, and then he phoned her teacher that evening.

qa.q: How did Paati see the situation?
qa.a: Paati could see the pushing was making things worse and that the girl needed time and quiet company.

grounding: Shows a parent learning that a child's clipped replies need a low-pressure moment, not demands, and acting the same day on what she shared.

passage: Vera stood in the kitchen doorway in Prague, fists tight. “I. Did. Not. Break. It.” She said each word slowly, pressing on every one. “I FOUND it like that.” Her mother, Freya, holding the pieces of the blue mug, opened her mouth to say, Don't use that tone. Then she stopped. Vera wasn't shouting; she was pressing on the words that mattered most to her. “Okay,” Freya said. “You found it broken. That's really important to you.” Vera's fists loosened. “Yes. Because Jakub said I did it.” Freya put the pieces down. “Let's go and ask Jakub, together.”

qa.q: What had broken?
qa.a: The blue mug had broken.

qa.q: What was Vera feeling as she pressed on every word?
qa.a: Vera felt angry and hurt at being blamed, and determined to be believed.

qa.q: What did Freya do instead of correcting Vera's tone?
qa.a: She repeated back what mattered to Vera and offered to ask Jakub together, treating the emphasis as importance, not rudeness.

qa.q: What would change if Freya had said “Don't use that tone”?
qa.a: Vera might feel unheard and more upset, and the question of who broke the mug would be lost in an argument about tone.

grounding: Shows a child stressing each word to show what matters most, and a parent reading the emphasis as importance rather than rudeness.

passage: At the end of practice at the football academy, Coach Nitin read out the goal scorers. “Two for Rohit, one for Aman.” Akash stepped forward, face flushed. “Coach, the second goal. I. Scored. That.” He said it slowly, hitting every word. A few boys whistled at his tone. Coach Nitin looked at him for a moment. Akash wasn't sulking; his chest was out, eyes bright, as if it mattered more than anything. Coach checked the video on his phone. “You're right. Your header. My mistake.” Akash's grin was enormous. “Thank you, Coach.”

qa.q: How did Coach Nitin check who scored?
qa.a: Coach Nitin checked the video on his phone.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he spoke slowly, hitting every word?
qa.a: Akash felt proud of his goal and upset that it was missed, so the emphasis showed how much it mattered.

qa.q: Why was checking the video a good response?
qa.a: It took Akash's emphasis seriously as a sign of what mattered and fixed the mistake fairly, instead of scolding his tone.

qa.q: How did the boys who whistled read Akash's tone?
qa.a: They heard it as cheeky or rude, not as pride about his goal.

grounding: Shows a child's emphatic speech carrying pride, and an adult reading it as what matters most rather than rudeness.

passage: I'm Tejas, and in debate practice Karthik was arguing that the school canteen should stop using plastic plates. Usually he mumbles. This time he slowed right down and leaned on every word: “We. Throw. Away. Four hundred. Plates. A day.” A couple of kids giggled, and one said, “Calm down, it's only practice.” I thought Sir might tell him off for sounding angry. But Sir wrote something down and said, “Karthik, which word matters most to you there?” Karthik said, “Four hundred.” Sir nodded. “Then that's the one to hit hardest.” I don't know what Karthik was feeling, but he didn't mumble again all afternoon.

qa.q: How many plates did Karthik say the canteen throws away each day?
qa.a: Karthik said they throw away four hundred plates a day.

qa.q: What might Karthik have been feeling as he leaned on every word?
qa.a: He probably felt strongly and a little angry about the waste, and the emphasis showed how much it mattered to him.

qa.q: How did Sir use Karthik's emphasis?
qa.a: Sir asked which word mattered most and told him to hit that one hardest, treating the emphasis as importance, not anger.

qa.q: How did Tejas expect Sir to react?
qa.a: Tejas expected Sir to tell Karthik off for sounding angry, and was surprised by Sir's question instead.

grounding: Shows a child slowing down and stressing words to show importance, and an adult reading emphasis as what matters most.

passage: I'm Amandeep. Last term, when our class plant was knocked off the windowsill, I asked Sonali, “Did you see who did it?” She didn't answer for ages. She looked at the floor, then at the door, then at me. I decided that meant she'd done it, and I said so, loudly. Her eyes filled. Later our teacher asked her calmly, “Is someone worried about getting into trouble?” Sonali nodded and whispered that a little Class 1 boy had done it by accident and was terrified. She'd been protecting him. I felt awful. Now when someone pauses before answering, I wait and ask a gentler question.

qa.q: What was knocked off the windowsill?
qa.a: The class plant was knocked off the windowsill.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling during her long pause?
qa.a: Sonali felt torn and worried, trying to protect a scared little boy who had knocked the plant over by accident.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that worked better than Amandeep's accusation?
qa.a: The teacher asked a calm, gentle question about whether someone was worried, which let Sonali explain.

qa.q: What was it like for the little Class 1 boy?
qa.a: The little boy was terrified of getting into trouble for an accident.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's hesitation as guilt, when she was protecting someone, and calm questions working better than accusation.

passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. Manoj, Class 6. When I asked Ujjwal where his homework was, there was a long pause. His eyes went to the window, and his hands tightened on the desk. A year ago I'd have called that a sign of an excuse being made up. Instead I asked quietly, “Is something making it hard to answer?” Another pause. Then Ujjwal said his mother has been on night shifts at the hospital this month, and he's been putting his little brother to bed. He was scared I'd send a note home and make her worry. I didn't. I gave him till Friday and asked the counsellor to check in with the family, gently.

qa.q: Where has Ujjwal's mother been working night shifts?
qa.a: She has been working night shifts at the hospital.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling during the long pause?
qa.a: Ujjwal was worried about the consequences, scared a note home would make his mother worry, not making up an excuse.

qa.q: Why did Manoj's quiet question work?
qa.a: It invited Ujjwal to explain without accusation, which brought out the real reason and led to fair help.

qa.q: How might Manoj once have read the pause?
qa.a: A year earlier, Manoj would have taken the pause as a sign of an excuse being made up.

grounding: Shows a teacher reading a child's hesitation as worry about consequences, not lying, and a calm follow-up question working.

passage: Thursday. Lalit's diary. At tabla class, Damini Ma'am asked, “Did you do your practice this week?” and I didn't answer straight away. I was trying to work out if twenty minutes counts when you're meant to do forty. Ma'am didn't say, “So you didn't.” She waited, then asked, “How much did you manage?” That made it easy. “Twenty. My palms got sore.” She said, “Thanks for telling me the real number,” and checked my hands. We decided I'd do two short practices a day instead of one long one. I'm writing this after the second one. My hands are fine.

qa.q: How long was Lalit meant to practise?
qa.a: Lalit was meant to practise for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling during the pause before answering?
qa.a: Lalit felt unsure and a little worried, wondering whether twenty minutes counted as doing the practice.

qa.q: Why did Damini Ma'am's follow-up question help?
qa.a: Asking how much Lalit managed made it easy to answer honestly, without feeling accused.

qa.q: What might Damini Ma'am have thought during the pause?
qa.a: She might have guessed Lalit was unsure rather than lying, which is why she waited and asked calmly.

grounding: Shows an adult reading a child's hesitation as uncertainty rather than lying, and a calm follow-up question getting an honest answer.

passage: Five minutes before the bell, Rajni Ma'am was still explaining the homework, and Abhinav had the answer to her earlier question burning in his mouth. At home, in his big noisy family, everyone talks over everyone; that's how you show you're listening. Here, he pressed his lips together. Ma'am said, “So for Friday, chapter…” He sat on his hands. Then he raised one. Ma'am finished her sentence, paused and nodded at him. “The answer was evaporation,” he said quickly. “Well done, and well waited,” Ma'am said, smiling. The bell rang. Abhinav let out a breath.

qa.q: How long was left before the bell?
qa.a: There were five minutes left before the bell.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling as he sat on his hands?
qa.a: Abhinav felt impatient and eager, bursting to share the answer but trying hard to wait.

qa.q: What steps did Abhinav use to hold back?
qa.a: He pressed his lips together, sat on his hands, raised one hand and waited for a pause.

qa.q: Why might talking over others feel natural to Abhinav?
qa.a: In his big, noisy family, overlapping talk shows you're listening, so waiting at school takes effort.

grounding: Shows a child holding back an interruption, raising a hand and waiting for a pause, while at home overlapping talk shows interest.

passage: At dinner in Sarita's Delhi flat, everyone talked at once. Sarita's father told a story, her brother cut in with the ending, her mother laughed over both of them, and Sarita shouted a correction. Jasleen sat with her spoon in the air, waiting for a gap. At home, her Biji said interrupting was the rudest thing a child could do. The gap never came. Twice she opened her mouth and closed it. Sarita's mother noticed. “Jasleen, beta, in this house if you wait for silence you'll wait till Diwali! Jump in, we like it.” Everyone laughed. Jasleen took a breath and said, loudly, “I have a funny story too.” They all stopped to listen.

qa.q: What did Jasleen's Biji say about interrupting?
qa.a: Biji said interrupting was the rudest thing a child could do.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling as she opened and closed her mouth?
qa.a: Jasleen felt awkward and left out, wanting to join in but held back by her family's rule about interrupting.

qa.q: How did Sarita's mother help Jasleen?
qa.a: She explained that in their house overlapping talk is welcome and invited Jasleen to jump in.

qa.q: What does talking over each other mean in Sarita's family?
qa.a: In Sarita's family it shows warmth and interest, not disrespect.

grounding: Shows a child raised to wait for a pause finding a family where overlapping talk shows warmth, and norms that vary between homes.

passage: “So the match was tied, and then Bhatia Sir—” “—threw the ball to me and I—” “Samir! I'm telling it!” Suraj glared at his little brother across the dinner table. “But I know the best bit!” “You always know the best bit. You never let me finish.” Their father put down his roti. “Samir, what could you do instead?” Samir squirmed. “Wait?” “And if you might burst?” “Raise my hand?” Suraj snorted. “At dinner?” “Why not,” said their father. “Or tap the table twice. Then Suraj finishes his sentence and hands it over.” Samir tapped twice. Suraj finished, “—and I caught it!” and nodded. “Now you.”

qa.q: What did their father put down?
qa.a: Their father put down his roti.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he glared at Samir?
qa.a: Suraj felt frustrated and annoyed that Samir kept taking over his story.

qa.q: What signal did the family agree on, and why does it help?
qa.a: Samir taps the table twice and waits for Suraj to finish, so he can show he wants a turn without cutting in.

qa.q: What was the dinner like for Samir?
qa.a: Samir was bursting with excitement to tell the best bit, which made waiting really hard for him.

grounding: Shows a child learning to hold back interruptions and signal for a turn instead of cutting in.

passage: The rain hadn't stopped all morning, the relay had been delayed twice, and the Blue House kids sat huddled under a dripping tarpaulin, soaked and grumpy. Then Kamal stood up and started the old house chant, stamping his feet: “Blue! Blue! Never give up, Blue!” One voice joined, then five, then the whole tent, stamping so the puddles jumped. Kamal felt the cold go out of him. Only Karthik, the new boy, sat with his lips shut, knees pulled up. A senior boy frowned. “Why aren't you chanting?” Kamal shook his head at him. “He's new. Let him watch.” Later, as they ran out into the rain, Karthik was stamping too, very quietly.

qa.q: What were the Blue House kids sitting under?
qa.a: They sat under a dripping tarpaulin.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling as the whole tent joined the chant?
qa.a: Kamal felt warm, lifted and connected, the cold going out of him as everyone joined in.

qa.q: Why was Kamal's answer to the senior boy wise?
qa.a: It protected the new boy from pressure, recognising he might be shy rather than disrespectful, and let him join in his own time.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Karthik under the tarpaulin?
qa.a: Karthik was new and probably shy, not ready to chant loudly with people he barely knew.

grounding: Shows a group chant lifting mood and belonging on a rainy sports day, and a child who does not join being shy rather than disrespectful.

passage: Every morning in the Mumbai school's assembly, four hundred voices sang the prayer together, and Jaya loved the way it filled her chest, like being part of something huge. Beside her, Madhuri only moved her lips. On Monday the PT teacher stopped beside them. “Madhuri, why aren't you singing? That's disrespectful.” Madhuri went red and stared at her shoes. At break Jaya asked her about it. “My voice cracks,” Madhuri whispered. “Last year someone laughed.” Jaya told the PT teacher, who nodded and said, “Quiet singing counts.” The next morning, Jaya stood a little closer and sang a little softer. Madhuri's voice came out, very small, under hers.

qa.q: How many voices sang the prayer each morning?
qa.a: Four hundred voices sang the prayer together.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling as the assembly sang?
qa.a: Jaya felt joyful and connected, as if part of something huge.

qa.q: How did Jaya help Madhuri join in?
qa.a: She asked privately, told the PT teacher, and stood closer singing softer so Madhuri's small voice could come out under hers.

qa.q: Why was Madhuri only moving her lips?
qa.a: Madhuri was shy about her cracking voice after being laughed at, not being disrespectful.

grounding: Shows group singing in assembly giving belonging, and a child who does not sing being shy, not disrespectful.

passage: “Come on, Rajni, sing with us!” Elizabeth grabbed her friend's hand as the carol group gathered by the church gate, lanterns swinging. “I don't know the words.” “Just sing la-la-la. Everyone does.” Rajni shook her head and stepped back. Elizabeth's aunt, holding the songbook, looked over. “Is she not joining? Doesn't she like our songs?” “No, Aunty, she likes them. She told me.” Elizabeth turned to Rajni. “Is it the words, or is it singing in front of people?” Rajni whispered, “People.” “Then walk with me and hold the lantern. That's part of it too.” Rajni took the lantern and smiled. By the third house, she was humming.

qa.q: What did Rajni hold during the carol walk?
qa.a: Rajni held the lantern.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she grabbed Rajni's hand?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt excited and eager to share the carols with her friend.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth offer instead of insisting, and why did it work?
qa.a: She offered Rajni the lantern to carry, which let her belong to the group without singing in front of people 🙂

qa.q: How did Elizabeth's aunt first read Rajni's silence?
qa.a: The aunt wondered if Rajni didn't like their songs, when really she was shy about singing in front of people.

grounding: Shows group singing as a source of belonging, and a child who declines to sing being shy rather than disrespectful.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Shalini. Keerthana has the squeakiest laugh in our class, like a toy duck. The first time I copied it, just the two of us on the swings, she laughed so hard she fell off, and we did duck laughs all the way home. So last month, in front of the whole class, I did it again when she answered a question. Everyone laughed. Keerthana didn't. She looked at her desk, and her ears went red. I'd been so busy with my joke that I hadn't looked at her. At break I said sorry. Now I only do the duck laugh when she starts it first.

qa.q: What does Shalini say Keerthana's laugh sounds like?
qa.a: Shalini says it sounds like a toy duck.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when the class laughed?
qa.a: Keerthana felt embarrassed and hurt, as her red ears and eyes on her desk showed.

qa.q: What rule did Shalini make, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Shalini only does the duck laugh when Keerthana starts it, so the imitation stays shared fun rather than mockery.

qa.q: Why did the same imitation feel different on the swings?
qa.a: On the swings it was just the two friends and Keerthana was laughing too, so it felt like play, not being made fun of.

grounding: Shows the same vocal imitation being affectionate play in private and unkind mimicry in public, with the target's reaction deciding.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: Class note, Friday. Binita, Class 5. At today's end-of-term party, Gurleen did an impression of me: hands on hips, high voice, “Settle DOWN, children, I can hear a PIN drop!” The class roared, and so did I. She looked at me first, checking, and when I laughed she did it again. That's affectionate play. Ten minutes later, another child copied the new boy's accent, and a few joined in. The new boy wasn't laughing. He was pulling at his sleeve. I stopped the game and said, “Copying is only funny if the person is laughing too. Look at faces first.” Gurleen nodded hardest. Before home time I sat with the new boy, and he's helping me with the notice board next week.

qa.q: What did Gurleen's impression of Binita say?
qa.a: She said, “Settle DOWN, children, I can hear a PIN drop!”

qa.q: What was the new boy likely feeling when others copied his accent?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and embarrassed, since he wasn't laughing and kept pulling at his sleeve.

qa.q: What rule did Binita give the class?
qa.a: Binita said copying is only funny if the person is laughing too, so look at faces first.

qa.q: How did Gurleen check that her impression was welcome?
qa.a: Gurleen looked at Binita first and only repeated it when Binita laughed.

grounding: Shows a child's affectionate imitation of a teacher next to unkind mimicry of a new pupil, and checking whether the target is laughing too.

subtype: Vocal imitation as humour or mockery [Mismatch]
passage: Saturday. Arohi's diary. At lunch I did my Vasudha Dadi impression: “Aye-aye-aye, so much salt, who made this?” Dadi laughed till she cried and said I got the eyebrows perfect. So I tried another one. My brother's voice keeps cracking, going high and low, so I copied it: “Pass the dal, pleeeease.” Nobody laughed. He put his spoon down and went to his room. Dadi said quietly, “With me, you knew I'd laugh. With him, you didn't look.” My face went hot. I knocked on his door and said sorry. He said, “Just don't do it in front of my friends.” Fair.

qa.q: What did Dadi say Arohi got perfect?
qa.a: Dadi said Arohi got the eyebrows perfect.

qa.q: What was Arohi's brother feeling when he put down his spoon?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt at having his cracking voice mocked in front of the family.

qa.q: What did Arohi do to repair things?
qa.a: Arohi knocked on his door and said sorry, and accepted his request not to do it in front of his friends.

qa.q: What was the difference between the two impressions for Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi enjoyed her own impression and laughed, but saw that the brother wasn't laughing, so that one was unkind.

grounding: Shows vocal imitation being loving fun with one person and hurtful mimicry with another, depending on the target's reaction.

passage: Seema, you're sulking because your friend walked past without saying hi. Let your Joseph Appachan tell you something. When I was eleven, in Kottayam, my best friend Mathew walked straight past me at the Sunday market. No wave, no smile, nothing. I was furious. I didn't speak to him for three days. On the fourth day I finally marched up and said, “Why did you ignore me?” He blinked. “When? I broke my glasses that week. I couldn't see anyone further than my own hand.” Three days of sulking, for nothing. So now I always look twice, and ask once, before I decide someone meant it.

qa.q: Why couldn't Mathew see young Joseph at the market?
qa.a: Mathew had broken his glasses that week.

qa.q: What was young Joseph feeling after Mathew walked past?
qa.a: He felt hurt and furious, believing his best friend had deliberately ignored him.

qa.q: What choice did Joseph finally make, and what did it show?
qa.a: He asked Mathew directly why he'd ignored him, which showed the missed hello was about broken glasses, not a snub.

qa.q: How might Mathew have felt during those three days?
qa.a: Mathew may have felt confused or hurt that his friend wasn't speaking to him, without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a child reading a missed greeting as a snub when it was inattention, and checking before feeling hurt.

passage: The corridor between periods was a crush of bags and elbows, and the bell had already gone. Nilesh spotted Gopika coming the other way, balancing a huge cardboard model of a heart, and called, “Hi, Gopika!” She walked straight past, eyes fixed on the model. Nilesh's smile dropped. Great. She's still annoyed about the cricket. He almost didn't look back. Then he did. She was edging sideways through the crowd, lips moving as if counting steps, one arm hooked round the model to keep it from being crushed. At lunch he asked, “Did you hear me this morning?” She stared. “You said hi? I didn't hear a thing. I was just trying not to drop the aorta.”

qa.q: What was Gopika carrying?
qa.a: Gopika was carrying a huge cardboard model of a heart.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when Gopika walked past?
qa.a: Nilesh felt hurt and snubbed, thinking she was still annoyed about the cricket.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that stopped him feeling hurt for nothing?
qa.a: He looked twice, noticed how hard she was concentrating on the model, and asked her at lunch.

qa.q: What was that moment in the corridor like for Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika was focused on not dropping the model in the crowd and never heard Nilesh's hello.

grounding: Shows a child reading an unanswered hello as a snub in a busy corridor, and checking twice before feeling hurt.

passage: Every morning in the lift of their Chandigarh apartment block, Baljeet said a big “Good morning!” to Francis Uncle from the seventh floor. Every morning, Francis Uncle only nodded, once, without a word. Baljeet began to think the old man didn't like children. Maybe I'm too loud. One Sunday, Baljeet watched from the balcony as Francis Uncle walked round the garden. He nodded at the guard, the gardener, the vegetable seller, even the dogs. The same short nod, the same small smile at the corner of his mouth. That evening, in the lift, Baljeet nodded first. Francis Uncle's eyes crinkled, and for the first time he said, “Good evening, young man.”

qa.q: Which floor does Francis Uncle live on?
qa.a: Francis Uncle lives on the seventh floor.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when Francis Uncle only nodded each morning?
qa.a: Baljeet felt unsure and a bit hurt, wondering if the old man didn't like children or found him too loud.

qa.q: How did Baljeet check his first reading?
qa.a: He watched Francis Uncle greet everyone with the same nod and small smile, and saw it was simply his friendly way.

qa.q: What might Francis Uncle have felt when Baljeet nodded first?
qa.a: Francis Uncle probably felt pleased and understood, since he answered with crinkled eyes and warm words.

grounding: Shows a child reading a neighbour's silent nod as coolness, and watching more to find it was his friendly way of acknowledging others.
